sections.title: How does the Average percentage calculator work?
sections.html:
The Average percentage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports average percentage (19) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (add more entries?); then you type in the percent boxes (numbered 1 to 4), the percent #1 (2), the sample size boxes (numbered 1 to 10) and the percent #3 (2).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Average percentage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Average percentage=((1 ÷ 2) × percent #1 + (1 ÷ 2) × percent #2)
Average percentage=((percent #1 × sample size #1 + percent #2 × sample size #2) ÷ (sample size #1 + sample size #2))
Average percentage=((1 ÷ 3) × percent #1 + (1 ÷ 3) × percent #2 + (1 ÷ 3) × percent #3)
Average percentage=((percent #1 × sample size #1 + percent #2 × sample size #2 + percent #3 × sample size #3) ÷ (sample size #1 + sample size #2 + sample size #3))
Average percentage=((1 ÷ 4) × percent #1 + (1 ÷ 4) × percent #2 + (1 ÷ 4) × percent #3 + (1 ÷ 4) × percent #4)
Average percentage=((percent #1 × sample size #1 + percent #2 × sample size #2 + percent #3 × sample size #3 + percent #4 × sample size #4) ÷ (sample size #1 + sample size #2 + sample size #3 + sample size #4))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Percent #1 = 10, Percent #2 = 10, Add more entries? set to Yes and How many? set to Two. The calculator returns Percent #1 = 10, Percent #2 = 10 and Average percentage = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Percent #1 = 10, Percent #2 = 10 and Average percentage = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Percent #1 = 10 and Percent #2 = 10.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Average percentage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the percent boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the sample size #1 and the sample size #2 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Average percentage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns average percentage (19), derived from the percent boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the sample size #1 and the sample size #2. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Average percentage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the percent boxes (numbered 1 to 6), the sample size #1 and the sample size #2, which is 23 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Percent #1 = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Average percentage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
